title: TRIAGE: Evaluating Prospective Metacognitive Control in LLMs under Resource Constraints
claim: Across many models and benchmarks, prospective planning efficiency falls well short of the oracle and is often worse than random.
layout: 4 stacked rows (benchmarks) by 19 models, grouped bars, shared legend on top
description: A wide grouped bar chart with four stacked panels, one per benchmark (AIME, GPQA, LCB, HLE). The x-axis lists 19 language models, from Qwen 2.5 3B to GPT-OSS 120B. Each model has four bars. Navy bars are standard inference and teal bars are extended reasoning. Solid bars show advisory efficiency (η_U) and hatched bars show binding efficiency (η_E). Thin whiskers show standard deviations. Dashed red lines mark the reference pass@1 accuracy. The y-axis runs from -2 to 1, with 'oracle' labelled at the top (1.0) and 'random' at 0. A legend row across the top explains the encodings. Most bars sit near or below zero, and hatched bars often drop far below it. A few models, such as GLM 5.1 and Kimi K2.5, reach high solid values.
caption: Triage efficiency across models and benchmarks under a shared budget (α = 0.5). Solid bars show advisory execution (ηU), hatched bars show binding allocations (ηE), and colors distinguish standard inference from extended reasoning. Bars show means over up to three planning runs; whiskers give sample standard deviations. Dashed red lines show reference pass@1 accuracy from the single-run comparison. Higher efficiency is better. Planning-run coverage and scoring details are provided in Additional Experiments.
abstract: Deploying language models as autonomous agents requires more than per-task accuracy: when an agent faces a queue of problems under a finite token budget, it must decide which to attempt, in what order, and how much compute to commit to each, all before any execution feedback is available. This is the prospective form of metacognitive control studied for decades in human cognition, yet whether language models possess it remains largely untested. We introduce TRIAGE, an evaluation framework in which a model receives a task pool and a token budget calibrated to its own baseline cost, and commits to a single ordered plan that jointly encodes selection, sequencing, and per-problem allocation. Plans are scored against an oracle built from the measured solvability and token costs of the model, using triage efficiency normalized between random and oracle performance, together with normalized regret relative to the oracle. We evaluate frontier and open-source models, with and without reasoning enabled, across competition mathematics, graduate-level science, code generation, and expert multidisciplinary knowledge, and find that current language models exhibit substantial gaps in prospective metacognitive control, revealing a previously unmeasured capability dimension with direct implications for resource-efficient agent deployment.
